standard.title: Australia's Development in Relation to the World by 1914
standard.description: the development of Australian society in relation to other nations in the world by 1914, including the effects of ideas and movements of people
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined Australian colonial development (AC9HH9K02–K06), Federation, and the social conditions of early 20th century Australia. They understand how Australian society developed and the key ideas and values that shaped it. This descriptor asks them to situate that development in an international context — assessing how Australia compared with other nations by 1914, particularly in terms of social legislation and women's rights.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the development of Australian society in relation to other nations by 1914, including the effects of ideas and movements of people on Australian development.

nodes.label: Social legislation and Australia's international position
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how the major social legislation of the new Federal Government affected living and working conditions and position Australia's reforms in an international context.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one piece of major social legislation passed by the new Federal Government and explain its effect on living or working conditions.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how major social legislation (Harvester Judgement, Immigration Restriction Act 1901, invalid and old-age pensions, maternity allowance scheme, Defence Act 1903) affected living and working conditions in Australia; situate these reforms in an international context — examining whether Australia was a world leader in social reform by 1914.
wider: Compare Australia's social welfare legislation by 1914 with that of comparable nations (e.g. Britain, New Zealand, USA) to assess whether Australia was genuinely a 'working man's paradise' or aligned with broader international reform trends

Examine the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 (the 'White Australia Policy') in international context — comparing it with immigration restriction in the USA (Chinese Exclusion Act) and Canada to assess how racial exclusion was a common feature of settler-colonial societies
nodes.hinge_reason: Situating Australian social legislation in international context is the core task of this descriptor. Without the comparative frame, students cannot assess whether Australia's reforms were distinctive or typical — and they lose the capacity to evaluate Australia's development as a nation-state.

response_modes.reason: The international comparison is the analytical move this descriptor demands. At least one comparative case — another nation's social legislation by 1914 — is needed to make the Australian position meaningful rather than self-referential.

success_criteria: Investigates at least two pieces of major Federal social legislation and explains their effects
Situates at least one Australian reform in an international context, with reference to another nation's comparable legislation

nodes.label: Women's roles and rights — continuities and changes by 1914
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain continuities and changes in the role of women in Australian society by 1914, including in women's rights, suffrage, political representation, and pacifism.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one continuity and one change in the role of women in Australia by 1914.
nodes.typical_width: Explain continuities and changes in women's roles including: the achievement of suffrage (1902) and its limits; women's political representation; women's contributions to pacifist and social reform movements; the persistence of restricted economic and social roles alongside new rights; investigate key women involved in these changes (e.g. Elizabeth Macquarie, Caroline Chisholm, Catherine Helen Spence, Louisa Lawson, Muriel Matters, Vida Goldstein).
wider: Examine the international suffrage movement and how Australian and New Zealand women connected with suffragists in Britain and the USA — assessing how ideas moved across national boundaries through movements of people and communication
Investigate the pacifist tradition in Australian women's movements before WWI and assess how this prepared the ground for women's activism during the conscription debates

Compare the rights and roles of women in Australia by 1914 with those in a non-Western society being studied (e.g. Qing China or Mughal India) to assess how Australian 'progressive' feminism was situated in a global context of women's rights

response_modes.reason: Examining multiple dimensions of women's experience — suffrage, pacifism, economic roles, key figures — prevents a simplified 'progress' narrative and shows the coexistence of achievement and continued restriction.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Women's roles and rights by 1914 connect the Australian domestic story to international networks and ideas — a rich site for exploring how social change operates through both legal reform and cultural movement, and how feminist ideas crossed national borders.
success_criteria: Explains at least one continuity and one change in women's roles in Australia by 1914, with reference to specific examples or figures
Connects at least one change in women's rights or roles to a broader international context or movement
